column2: A 'point estimator' is:
column3: The sample statistic used to estimate a population parameter
column4: The exact value of the population parameter
column5: A single data point from the sample
column6: A guess with no basis in data

column2: A 'point estimate' is:
column3: The specific numerical value of the statistic from one particular sample
column4: The name of the statistic being used
column5: The population parameter we're trying to find
column6: The average of all possible samples

column2: The difference between a point estimator and a point estimate is:
column3: The estimator is the statistic (like x-bar); the estimate is the number it produces (like 2.3)
column4: There is no difference — they mean the same thing
column6: The estimate always equals the parameter

column2: An estimator is 'unbiased' if:
column3: On average, the value of the estimator equals the population parameter
column4: Every single sample gives the correct value

column2: What does 'on average' mean in the definition of unbiased?
column3: Across ALL possible samples of the same size, the average value of the statistic equals the parameter
column6: When the sample is large enough

column2: A breeder has 5 dogs (ages 0, 2, 5, 8, 10). One sample of 3 gives x-bar = 2.3 while mu = 5. Does this single miss make x-bar a biased estimator?
column3: No — bias is about the average across ALL samples, not one sample
column5: Yes — the sample was too small
column6: It depends on the next sample

column2: In the Weimaraner example, the mean of ALL possible sample means equals 5, which is the population mean. This tells us:
column3: x-bar is an unbiased estimator of mu — it hits the target on average
column4: Every sample mean will be exactly 5
column5: The sample size was large enough

column2: Individual sample means vary from sample to sample. This natural variation is called:
column3: Sampling variability

column2: Sampling variability means that:
column3: Different random samples will give different values of the statistic
column4: The population is changing over time

column2: An estimator can be unbiased AND still give an estimate far from the parameter for a single sample. This is because:
column3: Unbiased refers to the long-run average, not any single result — variability is expected

column2: The sampling distribution of an unbiased estimator is:
column3: Centered at the population parameter

column2: If the sampling distribution of a statistic is NOT centered at the parameter, the statistic is:
column3: Biased

column2: The sample range of {0, 2, 5} from a population of {0, 2, 5, 8, 10} is:
The population range of {0, 2, 5, 8, 10} is:
In the Weimaraner example, the mean of ALL sample ranges is 7.8, but the population range is 10. This means the sample range is:
column3: A biased estimator — it doesn't hit the target on average
column4: An unbiased estimator — 7.8 is close to 10
column5: Unreliable because it's a small sample

column2: The sample range systematically UNDERESTIMATES the population range. Why?
column3: A sample can never produce a range LARGER than the population range — it can only be equal or smaller
column4: The formula for range is wrong
column5: Larger values are harder to measure
column6: Random chance makes it go either way

column2: Why can a sample range never exceed the population range?
column3: The sample is a subset of the population, so its max and min must be within the population's boundaries
column4: It can — this only happens with Weimaraners
column5: The range formula divides by n

column2: In the dot plot of all sample ranges, the dots cluster:
column3: To the LEFT of the population range — the sample range tends to be too small
column4: To the RIGHT of the population range
column5: Evenly on both sides of the population range

column2: A biased estimator that underestimates means:
column3: The sampling distribution is centered BELOW the true parameter value
column4: Every sample gives a value too low
column6: The sample size needs to be larger

column2: Could a statistic be biased in the OTHER direction — systematically overestimating?
column3: Yes — in principle, a statistic could be centered above the parameter
column5: Only if the population is skewed

column2: Which of these is an unbiased estimator of the population mean?
column3: The sample mean (x-bar)

column2: 'Estimators exhibit variability that can be modeled using probability.' This means:
column3: We can predict the pattern of variation across many samples, even though each sample is different
column5: We need probability to fix biased estimators
column6: Variability is always a problem to eliminate

column2: Two friends debate. Alex says: 'My sample mean was 2.3, not 5, so x-bar is biased.' Sam says: 'One miss doesn't make it biased.' Who is correct?
column3: Sam — bias is about the average of ALL possible samples, not one result

column2: If we could take ALL possible samples and calculate a statistic for each, we would create a:
column3: Sampling distribution

column2: To determine if an estimator is unbiased, you compare:
column3: The center (mean) of the sampling distribution to the population parameter
column4: One sample's estimate to the parameter
column5: The largest estimate to the smallest estimate
column6: The sample size to the population size

column2: A researcher takes one sample and gets a proportion of 0.47 for a population with p = 0.50. Can she conclude p-hat is biased?
column3: No — one sample isn't enough to judge bias; she'd need to consider all possible samples
column6: Only if she repeats the study

column2: Which analogy best captures what 'unbiased' means?
column3: An archer whose shots scatter around the bullseye — misses happen, but they average to the center
column4: An archer who hits the bullseye every single time
column5: An archer who always misses to the left
column6: An archer who misses by the same amount each time

column2: Using that same analogy, a BIASED estimator would be like:
column3: An archer whose shots consistently miss to one side of the bullseye
column5: An archer with a larger target
column6: An archer who takes fewer shots

column2: Why do we care about bias in statistics?
column3: A biased estimator will systematically miss the parameter — it can't be trusted to target the truth on average
column6: Bias only matters for large samples

column2: The sample mean is unbiased. The sample range is biased. What about the sample median — is it always unbiased?
column3: It depends on the population — the median is unbiased for symmetric populations but can be biased for skewed ones

column2: A statistic's bias and its variability are:
column3: Two separate things — a statistic can be unbiased but highly variable, or biased with low variability

column2: Which is worse: a statistic that is unbiased but very variable, or one that is biased but very precise?
column3: It depends on the situation — both bias and variability matter, and we ideally want low amounts of both

column2: If you increase the sample size, what happens to bias?
column3: Bias stays the same — if a statistic is unbiased at n=3, it's unbiased at n=100 too

column2: If you increase the sample size, what typically happens to variability?
column3: Variability decreases — larger samples give estimates closer to the parameter
